i.x: Have you ever known a person who turned his or her back on Christ and the church and simply walked away? Perhaps you have struggled to maintain your own Christian commitment in the face of disillusionment, spiritual confusion, loss of perspective, or outright persecution. The book of Hebrews points us to Christ. It provides light to help struggling Christians see Jesus clearly and stand firm.
Setting

As Christianity spread throughout the Mediterranean world, the first followers of Jesus Christ faced grave challenges. The Greco-Roman society misunderstood and mistrusted both Jews and Christians and considered them “atheists” because they did not believe in the Greek or Roman gods. Opposition to Christianity also arose from within traditional Judaism. Many Jews rejected Jesus as the Messiah. Those who converted to faith in Christ—from a Jewish or Gentile background—often paid a high price in their jobs, family connections, friendships, and other social associations. Persecution of Christians was common.

The believers to whom Hebrews was addressed probably belonged to a group of house churches in Rome in the early 60s AD. The Christian community in Rome was likely founded in the AD 30s when those present at Pentecost ([Acts 2:10](Acts.2.10)) made their way home. Roman believers had demonstrated courage and endurance ([Heb 10:32-34](Heb.10.32-Heb.10.34)), but by the time Hebrews was written, the spiritual fervor of some had grown cold ([5:11-14](Heb.5.11-Heb.5.14)), and their theological perspective was skewed ([2:1](Heb.2.1)). Some had even abandoned Christ and the church ([6:4-8](Heb.6.4-Heb.6.8)).
Summary

Hebrews is an energetic, well-crafted pastoral response to the needs of struggling people. In the style of a first-century sermon, the author alternates between *exposition* on the person and work of Christ and *exhortation* of the hearers to obedience and endurance. Through a detailed discussion on God’s Son, along with warnings, challenges, examples, and reminders of God’s faithfulness, the author calls the readers to persevere in following Christ.

Following an introduction to the whole sermon ([1:1-4](Heb.1.1-Heb.1.4)), the author’s exposition of Christ’s superiority develops in two great movements. The first movement ([1:5–2:18](Heb.1.5-Heb.2.18)) explains the Son’s relationship to the angels. The angels are servants ([1:6-7](Heb.1.6-Heb.1.7), [14](Heb.1.14)), but the exalted Son ([1:13](Heb.1.13)), with his unique relationship with the Father ([1:5](Heb.1.5)), is the Lord, creator, and sustainer of the universe—indeed, he is God ([1:8-12](Heb.1.8-Heb.1.12)). The author exhorts the hearers to pay careful attention to the message of salvation they have been taught ([2:1-4](Heb.2.1-Heb.2.4)), and then resumes the exposition. The exalted Christ’s position was temporarily lower than the angels when he became human ([2:5-9](Heb.2.5-Heb.2.9)); Jesus took on flesh and blood in order to die to set us free ([2:10-18](Heb.2.10-Heb.2.18)). The first exposition is followed by exhortation ([3:1–4:13](Heb.3.1-Heb.4.13)) that focuses on the need for faithful obedience and a continued promise of rest for God’s people.

The second movement of the exposition ([4:14–10:18](Heb.4.14-Heb.10.18)) addresses the position of the Son, our High Priest, in relation to the Old Testament sacrificial system. After introducing this theme [4:14-16](Heb.4.14-Heb.4.16), the author addresses the Son’s appointment as the superior High Priest ([5:1-10](Heb.5.1-Heb.5.10)) and confronts the community with their spiritual immaturity ([5:11–6:20](Heb.5.11-Heb.6.20)). A discussion of Melchizedek’s superiority to the Levitical priests ([7:1-10](Heb.7.1-Heb.7.10)) lays the groundwork for presenting Jesus as the superior High Priest according to the order of Melchizedek ([7:11-28](Heb.7.11-Heb.7.28)). In short, Jesus was not appointed according to the conventions of the Old Testament law, which said that priests should come from the tribe of Levi. Rather, he was appointed by God with an oath, on the basis of his indestructible life. The exposition then considers the superior offering of this appointed High Priest ([8:3–10:18](Heb.8.3-Heb.10.18)). Like the earthly priests, this superior priest had to make an offering for sins, but his offering was a new-covenant offering ([8:7-13](Heb.8.7-Heb.8.13)) that was superior to the old ([9:1–10:18](Heb.9.1-Heb.10.18)).

The final main section ([10:19–13:25](Heb.10.19-Heb.13.25)) is an exhortation that challenges the hearers to respond in faithfulness to the message about Christ. The book ends with a benediction and a formal conclusion ([13:20-25](Heb.13.20-Heb.13.25)).
Authorship

Unlike many other letters of the New Testament, Hebrews does not begin by identifying its author and recipients; many scholars today believe that this is because the book was originally written as a sermon. Since the earliest centuries of the church, the authorship of Hebrews has been much discussed. The book circulated with Paul’s letters, and some church fathers in the eastern half of the Mediterranean world (such as Origen and Clement of Alexandria) argued that Paul was the author. Others, especially around Rome, did not think Paul had written the book.

Almost all scholars today agree that Paul was not the author of Hebrews. First, in [2:3](Heb.2.3), the author is depicted as having received the Good News from the original witnesses who followed Christ, and this does not sound at all like Paul (see [Rom 1:1](Rom.1.1); [1 Cor 15:8](1Cor.15.8); [Gal 1:11-16](Gal.1.11-Gal.1.16)). Second, the style, theological images, and vocabulary are quite different from Paul’s; for example, Hebrews uses 169 words not found elsewhere in the New Testament.

Through the centuries, many other possible authors for the book have been suggested, such as Philip, Priscilla, Luke, Barnabas, Jude, and Clement of Rome. One of the most popular ideas, since Martin Luther first made the suggestion, is that Apollos wrote it. Luke describes Apollos in [Acts 18:24-26](Acts.18.24-Acts.18.26) as an eloquent man from Alexandria who was a powerful orator and preacher.

Although we cannot identify the author of Hebrews with certainty, a careful study of the book reveals much about them. First, the excellent Greek in which the book is written and its expertly crafted forms of expression point to a highly educated person. Second, the author of Hebrews must have been a dynamic preacher, one trained in interpretation and exposition, who had memorized large portions of the Old Testament. Third, and most importantly, this author was a deeply concerned Christian leader who addressed their readers urgently and with passion. Hebrews is not simply a theological treatise, but a pastoral appeal that vies for the hearts and minds of those who are struggling in their Christian commitment.
Recipients

The author writes, “Greet all your leaders and all the believers there. The believers from Italy send you their greetings” ([Heb 13:24](Heb.13.24)). The author seems to have been writing back to Italy, and probably to Rome, sending greetings from Italian Christians who had traveled abroad.

Those addressed in this letter seem to have had some background in Jewish worship. The author’s use of the Old Testament and the theological concepts that are presented would have been familiar to those of the synagogue in the Mediterranean world. This does not necessarily mean that all of the recipients were Jews, since many Gentiles were part of the synagogue as “God-fearers” who worshiped the God of Israel.
Occasion of Writing

Some in the Christian community were evidently struggling to maintain their commitment as they were being persecuted. Passages such as [Hebrews 10:32-39](Heb.10.32-Heb.10.39) suggest that this group of believers, which had faced persecution in the past, was facing it again. In the crucible of having to stand for Christ and the church in the face of public opposition, some were faltering spiritually and others had apparently turned their backs on the faith altogether. The author thus challenges this group of professed Christ followers to endure in their public profession of Christ.

If we are correct that Rome is the destination for this book, this word of exhortation might have been precipitated by the persecution that occurred under the emperor Nero, whose intense persecution and martyrdom of Christians in the mid-60s AD is well known. It is also possible that Hebrews was written after AD 70. This seems less likely, however, because at the time Hebrews was written, apparently no one in the community had faced martyrdom (see [12:4](Heb.12.4)), but the pressure of persecution was on the rise.
Meaning and Message

God has spoken about his Son and through his Son ([1:1-3](Heb.1.1-Heb.1.3)), and there are dire consequences for those who do not listen and respond with obedience to that word ([2:1-3](Heb.2.1-Heb.2.3)). In the end, Jesus, the creator and sustainer of the universe ([1:2-3](Heb.1.2-Heb.1.3)), will put away the created order like a person rolls up an article of old clothing ([1:10-12](Heb.1.10-Heb.1.12)).

Jesus is supremely worthy of our commitment, worship, and endurance in the faith. He is superior to the angels ([1:5-14](Heb.1.5-Heb.1.14)), to Moses ([3:1-6](Heb.3.1-Heb.3.6)), and to the Levitical priesthood of the old covenant ([5:1-10](Heb.5.1-Heb.5.10); [7:1-28](Heb.7.1-Heb.7.28)).

Jesus has made a new, heavenly covenant, offering himself once for all through his own death ([8:3–10:18](Heb.8.3-Heb.10.18)). In his incarnation he endured as a faithful Son ([3:1-6](Heb.3.1-Heb.3.6); [5:7-8](Heb.5.7-Heb.5.8); [12:1-2](Heb.12.1-Heb.12.2)), and in his exaltation he reigns as the supreme Lord of the universe ([1:2-4](Heb.1.2-Heb.1.4), [8-13](Heb.1.8-Heb.1.13)). Jesus thus provides us with a superior basis for persevering in the Christian life and having hope for the future.

We can also look to positive examples of others who have been faithful in their journey to God’s eternal city (see [6:13-15](Heb.6.13-Heb.6.15); [10:32-39](Heb.10.32-Heb.10.39); [11:1-40](Heb.11.1-Heb.11.40)), and to negative examples of those who fell through disobedience (see [3:7-19](Heb.3.7-Heb.3.19); [6:4-8](Heb.6.4-Heb.6.8)). And we can embrace God’s promises to us concerning our inheritance as his children ([4:3-11](Heb.4.3-Heb.4.11); [6:13-20](Heb.6.13-Heb.6.20); [12:22-24](Heb.12.22-Heb.12.24)).

Because of Jesus, we can live as faithful members of the Christian community in our relationships and in our worship ([13:1-17](Heb.13.1-Heb.13.17)). Our perseverance in the Christian faith will be directly proportional to the clarity with which we understand who Jesus is and what he has accomplished on our behalf.

b.x: Ancient sermons often began with an introduction meant to grab the hearer’s attention and introduce the sermon’s main topics. In Hebrews, the first four verses form a single, eloquent Greek sentence built around the main clause, **God . . . has spoken**. Most English translations present these verses as several sentences for ease of reading.
**Long ago. . . . And now:** These verses deal with two time periods in which God has spoken, addressing the differences between the two eras in parallel fashion.

**Long ago** referred to the time before the Messiah’s coming. For the author of Hebrews, this primarily meant the Old Testament era. Throughout that past era, **God spoke many times and in many ways**—through dreams, visions, mighty acts, stories, commands, exhortations, angelic appearances, and appearances of God himself.
**The prophets** were all those through whom God gave his revelation (see [2 Pet 1:19-21](2Pet.1.19-2Pet.1.21)).

**These final days** refers to the historical era inaugurated at Christ’s coming (see [Isa 2:2](Isa.2.2); [Acts 2:17](Acts.2.17)). Whereas the revelation of the Old Testament era came in a wide variety of forms over time, God’s ultimate revelation was given **through his Son***,* Jesus (see [Heb 2:3-4](Heb.2.3-Heb.2.4)).
**as an inheritance:** Christ is God’s royal heir; the author probably had [Ps 2:8](Ps.2.8) in mind.

The word translated **radiates***,* found only here in the New Testament, includes an idea of intense brightness. **God’s own glory** is the glorious manifestation of his presence ([Exod 16:7](Exod.16.7); [33:18](Exod.33.18); [Isa 40:5](Isa.40.5)). The Son’s glory is an expression of God’s glory—the Son of God manifests the person and presence of God ([Luke 9:32](Luke.9.32); [John 1:14](John.1.14); [2:11](John.2.11); [17:5](John.17.5); [Rom 8:17](Rom.8.17)).

The term translated **expresses***,* used only here in the New Testament, was used of a distinguishing mark imprinted on an object such as a coin. The Son gives a clear picture of **the very character of God** ([John 1:18](John.1.18); [Phil 2:6](Phil.2.6); [Col 1:15](Col.1.15)).

**the mighty power of his command** (literally *his powerful word*): God’s word is the powerful, dynamic force that created and governs the world ([Heb 11:3](Heb.11.3); [Ps 33:6-11](Ps.33.6-Ps.33.11)). Elsewhere the Son is called “the Word of God” ([Rev 19:13](Rev.19.13); see also [John 1:1-18](John.1.1-John.1.18)).
**cleansed us from our sins:** See [Heb 9:11–10:18](Heb.9.11-Heb.10.18).

**he sat down:** This clause is an allusion to [Ps 110:1](Ps.110.1) (see also [Heb 1:13](Heb.1.13); [8:1](Heb.8.1); [10:12](Heb.10.12); [12:2](Heb.12.2)), which foretold the exaltation of Christ after his suffering (see [Matt 22:44](Matt.22.44); [Acts 2:33](Acts.2.33); [1 Cor 15:25](1Cor.15.25)). **The right hand** of God indicates high honor, rank, and position (see [1 Kgs 2:19](1Kgs.2.19); [Pss 16:11](Ps.16.11); [45:4](Ps.45.4), [9](Ps.45.9); [80:17](Ps.80.17)).

The Son’s exalted position **shows that the Son is far greater than the angels** in status or rank. First-century Jews were fascinated with angels and held them in high esteem, so the author of Hebrews establishes the Son’s superiority to them.

**just as the name . . . is greater:** Cp. [2 Sam 7:8-14](2Sam.7.8-2Sam.7.14). Some commentators believe that the title “Son” is the *name* implied here. Others think the name is *Yahweh,* the covenant name of God in the Old Testament ([Exod 3:14-15](Exod.3.14-Exod.3.15); cp. [Phil 2:9-11](Phil.2.9-Phil.2.11)).

In these ten verses, the author uses a variety of Old Testament texts to show that Jesus is superior to the angels. Among ancient Jewish and Christian interpreters, Old Testament passages were strung together one after the other in “chain quotations” (called “pearl stringing”) to convince the hearers or readers of a certain theological point by presenting a lot of scriptural evidence together.

**God . . . said:** This verse quotes [Ps 2:7](Ps.2.7) and [2 Sam 7:14](2Sam.7.14). By exalting Jesus to his right hand (see [Acts 1:9-11](Acts.1.9-Acts.1.11); [2:32-36](Acts.2.32-Acts.2.36); [7:55-56](Acts.7.55-Acts.7.56)), the Father proclaimed his unique relationship with the Son.

**Today I have become your Father** (or *Today I reveal you as my Son*): Jesus did not *become* the Son at the exaltation—he had been involved in creation ([Heb 1:2](Heb.1.2))—but the exaltation verified his identity to all.

The **supreme** (or *firstborn*) **Son** shared the authority of the father, inherited most of his property, and was especially favored. In the New Testament, “firstborn” most frequently refers to Christ’s supremacy both in the church and in the created order; his resurrection is often given as the evidence for this status ([Acts 13:33](Acts.13.33); [Rom 1:4](Rom.1.4); [8:29](Rom.8.29); [Col 1:15](Col.1.15), [18](Col.1.18); [Rev 1:5](Rev.1.5); cp. [Heb 12:23](Heb.12.23), where believers are called firstborn children).
**“Let all of God’s angels worship him”:** This quotation from [Deut 32:43](Deut.32.43) demonstrates the lower status of the angels in that they worship the Son (see also [Ps 97:7](Ps.97.7)).
This verse quotes [Ps 104:4](Ps.104.4) to show that the angels are messengers or **servants** and, therefore, of a lesser rank than the Son, whom they serve.

In the Old Testament, **angels** are sometimes associated with **winds** and **fire** (see [Exod 3:2](Exod.3.2); [Judg 6:21](Judg.6.21); [13:16](Judg.13.16), [20](Judg.13.20); [2 Sam 22:11](2Sam.22.11); [Pss 18:10](Ps.18.10); [35:5](Ps.35.5)), which is why angels are mentioned in connection with God’s lordship over nature.
These verses, quoting [Ps 45:6-7](Ps.45.6-Ps.45.7), proclaim **the Son** as the divine, just, eternal, anointed King of the universe.
**to the Son he says:** Jesus is addressed as **God**; in [Heb 1:9](Heb.1.9), **your God** is a reference to God the Father.

**pouring out the oil of joy:** Olive oil was used to anoint kings of Israel at the inauguration of their rule ([1 Sam 10:1](1Sam.10.1); [1 Kgs 19:15-16](1Kgs.19.15-1Kgs.19.16)). God **has anointed** his Son, Jesus Christ, as King.

These verses, quoting [Ps 102:25-27](Ps.102.25-Ps.102.27), celebrate the Son as both the creator and the one who brings the created order to an end. All created things **will wear out like old clothing***,* and the Son will **discard them** (cp. [Heb 2:5](Heb.2.5); [2 Pet 3:13](2Pet.3.13); [Rev 21:1](Rev.21.1)). By contrast, the Son of God **will live forever**.

In climactic fashion, the author ends his string of Old Testament quotations (see study note on 1:5-14) by quoting from [Ps 110:1](Ps.110.1) in celebration of Christ’s exaltation (see also study notes on Luke 20:42-43; 22:69; 1 Cor 15:25; Eph 1:19-22).

The image of the Son’s **enemies** as **a footstool under** his **feet** represents their absolute subjugation (see [Heb 2:8](Heb.2.8)). In the ancient world, a victorious king would place his foot on the neck or back of an enemy as a symbolic act of domination.

**Therefore, angels are only servants:** The author restates his conclusion. God sends out the angels **to care for** his people, **who will inherit salvation** at the end of the age (see [9:28](Heb.9.28)).

The author makes an argument from lesser to greater: If, in the lesser situation of the Old Testament era, people who rejected God’s word as delivered by angels were severely punished, how much greater the punishment will be for those who now reject the word of salvation that has been delivered by the Son himself and confirmed by the Holy Spirit.
**The truth we have heard** is the message of salvation delivered through Christ ([2:3](Heb.2.3)).
**Drift away** pictures a ship getting off course. Here it speaks of getting off track spiritually due to not listening **very carefully** to the Good News.
According to Jewish tradition, **the message God delivered,** the law given on Mount Sinai (see [Acts 7:38](Acts.7.38); [Gal 3:19](Gal.3.19)), was delivered **through angels**.

**Violation of the law** was punished (see [Exod 22:19](Exod.22.19); [Lev 20:10](Lev.20.10); [Num 35:16-21](Num.35.16-Num.35.21)), and punishment was inescapable ([Prov 1:24-31](Prov.1.24-Prov.1.31); [Jer 11:11](Jer.11.11)).

**So what makes us think we can escape?** Here the author presses the full force of the danger of turning away from Christ and his salvation. There is no escape from punishment for those who walk away, and the punishment will be of the greatest severity (cp. [6:4-12](Heb.6.4-Heb.6.12); [10:26-31](Heb.10.26-Heb.10.31); [12:29](Heb.12.29); [Rom 2:5](Rom.2.5); [1 Thes 2:16](1Thess.2.16)).

**Salvation** refers to God’s acts on behalf of his people. For example, God saved his people through the exodus from Egypt ([Deut 26:5-9](Deut.26.5-Deut.26.9)). In the New Testament, salvation primarily refers to Christ’s work of rescuing people from the penalty of sin and giving them new life by his sacrificial death on the cross ([Heb 5:9-10](Heb.5.9-Heb.5.10)). This salvation was **first announced by the Lord Jesus himself** (e.g., [Matt 4:17](Matt.4.17); [9:35](Matt.9.35); [Mark 1:15](Mark.1.15); [Luke 13:1-5](Luke.13.1-Luke.13.5)). He **then delivered** (or *validated*) the message through **those who heard him speak** (e.g., [Mark 6:12](Mark.6.12); [Acts 2:38](Acts.2.38); [3:19-20](Acts.3.19-Acts.3.20)).

**God confirmed the message** (literally *God bore witness*): God himself confirmed the validity of the message of Christ and his followers **by giving signs and wonders and various miracles and gifts of the Holy Spirit** (see [Acts 2:22](Acts.2.22); [Rom 15:19](Rom.15.19); [2 Cor 12:12](2Cor.12.12)).

The author of Hebrews uses [Ps 8:4-6](Ps.8.4-Ps.8.6) to transition from the discussion of Christ’s exalted divinity ([Heb 1:5-14](Heb.1.5-Heb.1.14)) to the discussion of his humanity ([2:10-18](Heb.2.10-Heb.2.18)). [Psalm 8](Ps.8.1-Ps.8.9) is often presented with [Ps 110:1](Ps.110.1) (see [Heb 1:13](Heb.1.13)) to speak of the submission of created things to Christ (see [1 Cor 15:25-27](1Cor.15.25-1Cor.15.27); [Eph 1:20-23](Eph.1.20-Eph.1.23)). Christ is the consummate human being. In his exaltation, he fulfills what fallen humanity could not: true dominion over the created order.
**it is not angels:** Cp. [1:13](Heb.1.13).

These verses quote [Ps 8:4-6](Ps.8.4-Ps.8.6). [Psalm 8](Ps.8.1-Ps.8.9) speaks of the position God has given humanity, but the author of Hebrews applies it as a prediction about Christ, who is the fulfillment and representative head of humanity.
**What are mere mortals:** These two lines of the psalm proclaim God’s special attention to human beings.

**a son of man** (or *the Son of Man*): The phrase *son of man* speaks of human existence; it parallels *mere mortals* in the previous line. In the Gospels Jesus frequently referred to himself with this phrase.
**them:** Literally *him.* This refers to humanity in general and is applied specifically to Christ (see study note on 2:6-8).

Christ became **a little lower than the angels** (or *lower than the angels for only a little while*), like other human beings (see also [Phil 2:5-8](Phil.2.5-Phil.2.8)). As a result of his suffering, he was **crowned** . . . **with glory and honor** (see [Heb 2:9](Heb.2.9); [Phil 2:9-11](Phil.2.9-Phil.2.11)).
**You gave them authority over all things** (literally *You have put all things under his feet*): See study note on 2:6-8.
**nothing is left out:** All things are ultimately subject to Christ and the church, but **we have not yet seen** the complete expression of this reality—it will be consummated at the end of the age.

**What we do see is Jesus:** How can the church persevere when evil and death are still in the world? We look to Jesus both in his human life in **a position “a little lower than the angels”** and in his exaltation, **now “crowned with glory and honor.”** His suffering as a human being led to his exaltation (see [Phil 2:5-11](Phil.2.5-Phil.2.11); cp. [Isa 52:13–53:12](Isa.52.13-Isa.53.12)). See also [Heb 12:1-13](Heb.12.1-Heb.12.13).

At least four reasons why the Son of God became human are implied in this passage. First, **it was only right:** It is consistent with what we know of God’s character that he would accomplish salvation in this way ([2:10](Heb.2.10)). Second, Jesus had to become **human** to die ([2:14](Heb.2.14)). Third, high priests, as detailed in the Old Testament law, had to come from among God’s **people** ([2:17](Heb.2.17)). Fourth, Jesus became a sympathetic priest, experiencing the **suffering and testing** we know as humans ([2:18](Heb.2.18)).

**children** (literally *sons*): The author plays off his use of the title *Son* for Jesus throughout the section, here referring to the people of God as *sons.* The translation *children* makes it clear that this term refers to all God’s people, male and female.

The term translated **leader** had a wide range of meanings in the ancient world, including *founder,* *hero,* *champion, prince, captain, leader,* or *scout.* Jesus is a leader in that he blazed a trail for those who are saved, leading them to glory.

**have the same Father** (literally *are all out of one*): Based on the family terminology in the context, the phrase can be understood as referring to God. However, the author might have been thinking of Abraham as a common ancestor (see [2:16](Heb.2.16)) or of human nature as a common experience (*out of one nature*).
**brothers and sisters:** Greek *adelphoi,* a generic term that refers to members of the same family, both male and female.

This verse quotes [Ps 22:22](Ps.22.22), commenting on the phrase **brothers and sisters** in [Heb 2:11](Heb.2.11). [Psalm 22](Ps.22.1-Ps.22.31) contains profound messianic prophecies concerning the sufferings of Christ ([Ps 22:1](Ps.22.1), [7-8](Ps.22.7-Ps.22.8), [16-18](Ps.22.16-Ps.22.18); see [Matt 27:35](Matt.27.35), [43](Matt.27.43); [John 19:23-24](John.19.23-John.19.24), [31-36](John.19.31-John.19.36)). [Psalm 22:22](Ps.22.22) shows the solidarity of the righteous sufferer (Jesus) with the people of God in praising God for his help.
This verse quotes [Isa 8:17-18](Isa.8.17-Isa.8.18), which comes from a broader messianic context (cp. [Isa 8:14](Isa.8.14) with [Rom 9:33](Rom.9.33); [1 Pet 2:8](1Pet.2.8)).
**I will put my trust in him** here declares Jesus’ trust in the Father.
**I and the children God has given me** indicates a close relationship between Jesus and the children of God.
The death of **the Son** of God as a sacrifice for sin served to **break the power of the devil:** It made the devil’s **power of death** ineffective ([1 Cor 15:56](1Cor.15.56)).

Philo, a first-century Jewish philosopher, wrote that “nothing is so calculated to enslave the mind as fearing death” (Philo, *That Every Good Person Is Free* 3.22). Through his sacrificial death, Christ set free those who were **slaves to the fear of dying**.
**descendants of Abraham:** Jesus’ sacrifice on the cross was for the heirs of God’s promises to Abraham, rather than for the **angels**.
These verses introduce Jesus’ role as **our merciful and faithful High Priest***,* which is fully discussed in the central section of Hebrews ([4:14–10:25](Heb.4.14-Heb.10.25)).
**It was necessary for him** to share our humanity (see [5:1](Heb.5.1)).

The author compares Jesus to Moses, setting Jesus forward as the supreme example of faithfulness. The great status of Moses, a revered figure in Judaism, is used to show the incomparable greatness of Jesus.

**dear brothers and sisters who belong to God:** Literally *holy brothers.* Speakers and writers of the ancient world often addressed religious gatherings as “brothers” (Greek *adelphoi*), referring to both men and women.
**think carefully about this Jesus:** Focusing on Jesus is a primary means of persevering in the faith ([2:9](Heb.2.9); [12:1-2](Heb.12.1-Heb.12.2)).

**God’s messenger** (literally *God’s apostle*): This description might be highlighting the Son’s role in bearing a proclamation of God’s name and message ([2:12](Heb.2.12); [Matt 10:40](Matt.10.40); [Mark 9:37](Mark.9.37); [Luke 10:16](Luke.10.16)).

Jesus **was faithful to God** and to the task to which the Father had appointed him ([5:7-10](Heb.5.7-Heb.5.10); [12:1-3](Heb.12.1-Heb.12.3); [Phil 2:5-11](Phil.2.5-Phil.2.11)), **just as Moses** had been ([Num 12:7](Num.12.7)). Many Jews of the first century regarded Moses as the greatest person in history, of even higher status than the angels.

**Jesus deserves far more glory** for two reasons. First, **a person who builds a house deserves more praise than the house itself**. The Messiah is the one who builds God’s house (see [2 Sam 7:13](2Sam.7.13)). The implication is that Moses is part of the house (i.e., God’s people) that God has built. Second, whereas Moses was **a servant** in God’s house, **Christ, as the Son,** is the heir **in charge of God’s entire house**. Sons have greater status than household servants.

We are part of Christ’s house **if we keep our courage**. The author could not give unqualified assurance to those who were drifting away from Christ and the church. Those who persevere in the faith have assurance that they are part of God’s house (see [3:14](Heb.3.14); [Rom 8:9](Rom.8.9), [17](Rom.8.17); [11:22](Rom.11.22); [2 Cor 13:5](2Cor.13.5); [Col 1:22-23](Col.1.22-Col.1.23)).

This passage presents, “as a warning to us” ([1 Cor 10:6](1Cor.10.6)), the negative example of those who wandered in the wilderness for forty years and died there. The wilderness wanderings represent disobedience to God and its consequences (see [Num 32:7-11](Num.32.7-Num.32.11); [Deut 1:19-35](Deut.1.19-Deut.1.35); [Ps 106:24-26](Ps.106.24-Ps.106.26)).

**Israel** . . . **rebelled** and **tested** God in places such as Massah and Meribah, where there was a shortage of water ([Exod 17:1-7](Exod.17.1-Exod.17.7); [Num 20:2-13](Num.20.2-Num.20.13)), and especially at Kadesh, where the disobedient Israelites refused to enter the Promised Land ([Heb 3:10](Heb.3.10); see [Num 14:1-25](Num.14.1-Num.14.25); [Deut 1:19-46](Deut.1.19-Deut.1.46); [Ps 106](Ps.106.1-Ps.106.48)).

Despite seeing the **miracles** God had performed on their behalf, the people of Israel **tested** God’s **patience** by refusing to trust him in the wilderness ([Num 14:11](Num.14.11), [22](Num.14.22)). The essence of their rebellion was that **their hearts always** turned **away** from God—they did not desire to obey him. The result was that God **was angry with them**.
Rebellion has consequences.
God’s **anger** is not merely an emotional reaction; it is his just displeasure toward sin ([John 3:36](John.3.36); [Rom 1:18](Rom.1.18); [1 Thes 2:16](1Thess.2.16)).

God’s **oath** (see [Heb 6:13-20](Heb.6.13-Heb.6.20); [7:20-22](Heb.7.20-Heb.7.22), [28](Heb.7.28)) was that they would **never enter** Canaan, the **place of rest** from their wanderings ([Deut 1:19-46](Deut.1.19-Deut.1.46); [3:20](Deut.3.20); [12:10](Deut.12.10); [Josh 1:13](Josh.1.13)).

The author of Hebrews discusses the terms *heart, day, today, hear, enter, rest, unbelief,* and *oath,* all drawn from [Ps 95](Ps.95.1-Ps.95.11). Bible teachers of the ancient world would cite and then explain an Old Testament text, often highlighting significant words from the text, just as preachers do today. This form of exposition was called *midrash.*
**hearts . . . not evil and unbelieving:** An evil heart stubbornly sets its will against the Lord due to unbelief, causing a person to turn **away from the living God**.
Using the word **“today”** from [Ps 95:7](Ps.95.7), the author challenges his hearers to **warn each other every day** against the deceptive and hardening power of **sin**.

**For if we are faithful:** Those who persevere in the faith have assurance that they are indeed part of God’s family (see [3:6](Heb.3.6); [Rom 8:9](Rom.8.9), [17](Rom.8.17); [11:22](Rom.11.22); [2 Cor 13:5](2Cor.13.5); [Col 1:22-23](Col.1.22-Col.1.23)).

This verse again quotes [Ps 95:7-8](Ps.95.7-Ps.95.8), the exhortation from that portion of the psalm. It sums up the author’s own exhortation in [Heb 3:12-14](Heb.3.12-Heb.3.14), focusing on the importance of listening and responding favorably to God’s **voice**.

These verses contain a rapid-fire series of questions and answers, a common rhetorical technique. The three questions follow the progression of ideas found in [Ps 95:8-11](Ps.95.8-Ps.95.11): The people of Israel rebelled against God, God was angry, and God took an oath that they would never enter his rest. The answers are taken from other Old Testament passages that focus on the Israelites’ rebellion in the wilderness ([Num 14](Num.14.1-Num.14.45); [Deut 9](Deut.9.1-Deut.9.29); [Ps 106](Ps.106.1-Ps.106.48)). The author drives home the terrible cost of disobedience to God.

**Unbelief** and disobedience are closely associated in Hebrews and in the Old Testament passages being discussed ([Num 14:11](Num.14.11); [Deut 9:23](Deut.9.23); [Ps 78:22](Ps.78.22), [32](Ps.78.32)). As a consequence of disobedience, **they were not able to enter his rest** by entering the land of Canaan ([Deut 3:20](Deut.3.20); [12:10](Deut.12.10); [Josh 1:13](Josh.1.13)).

The author transitions to the **promise** that the faithful will enter God’s **rest** and exhorts his listeners to take this promise seriously. Hearing is not enough: It must be combined with **faith**.
To **fear** God means to experience an appropriate reverence, even awe, for God and his will. It would be the worst of tragedies to **fail to experience** what God has promised.
**This good news** is the message of salvation ([2:3-4](Heb.2.3-Heb.2.4)).

**they didn’t share the faith of those who listened to God:** Some manuscripts read *they didn’t combine what they heard with faith.* In either case, the hearers were deficient in faith, distrusting God’s word of promise.
People **who believe** the Good News are the true heirs of God’s **rest***,* the salvation that God offers through Christ’s sacrifice.

**God said:** The quotation of [Ps 95:11](Ps.95.11) reminds the reader that the unbelieving rebels in the wilderness would **never enter** God’s **place of rest** (cp. [Heb 11:8](Heb.11.8), [10](Heb.11.10), [14-16](Heb.11.14-Heb.11.16); [12:22-24](Heb.12.22-Heb.12.24)).
**since he made the world:** God’s rest means much more than physical entry into Canaan (see study note on 4:4).
This verse quotes [Gen 2:2](Gen.2.2) to demonstrate that the promised rest was established when **God rested** at creation.
This quotation of [Ps 95:11](Ps.95.11) reiterates the point made in [Heb 4:3](Heb.4.3).

**So God’s rest is there:** Building on the discussion in [4:3-5](Heb.4.3-Heb.4.5), the author is about to argue that the promised **rest** is still available ([4:7-10](Heb.4.7-Heb.4.10)). But those who wandered in the wilderness, even though they **heard** the **good news** that the Promised Land was open to them, **failed to enter because they disobeyed God** (see [Num 14:1-25](Num.14.1-Num.14.25); [Deut 1:19-46](Deut.1.19-Deut.1.46); [Ps 106](Ps.106.1-Ps.106.48)).

**So God set another time . . . and that time is today:** The logic here is that **David** wrote [Ps 95](Ps.95.1-Ps.95.11) **much later** than the wilderness debacle, so God’s **rest** cannot be limited to that earlier generation. The **words already quoted** are from [Ps 95:7-8](Ps.95.7-Ps.95.8); these words encourage us not to **harden** our **hearts** when hearing God’s **voice** so that we might enter the rest that the people in the wilderness were denied. This opportunity is available **today** (see [Heb 3:13](Heb.3.13)).

**Joshua** is the same name as *Jesus* (Greek *Iēsous,* Hebrew *Yehoshua‘*). It is normally translated *Joshua* in the Old Testament and *Jesus* in the New Testament (see also study note on Exod 17:9). The author is making a word play on Jesus’ and Joshua’s shared name. Joshua did lead God’s people into the Promised Land ([Josh 3–4](Josh.3.1-Josh.4.24)), but God had more in mind when he promised his people **rest**. God’s ultimate rest is provided by Jesus ([Heb 3:13-14](Heb.3.13-Heb.3.14); [4:3](Heb.4.3), [9-11](Heb.4.9-Heb.4.11), [14-16](Heb.4.14-Heb.4.16)).

**a special rest:** Jesus’ sacrifice functioned as a Day of Atonement sacrifice ([5:1-3](Heb.5.1-Heb.5.3); [9:13-22](Heb.9.13-Heb.9.22); see [Lev 23:26-28](Lev.23.26-Lev.23.28), [32](Lev.23.32)). Through Christ’s sacrifice, God’s promised rest for his people is available.
**have rested from their labors:** See [Exod 20:8-11](Exod.20.8-Exod.20.11).
**just as God did:** [Gen 2:2](Gen.2.2).

**let us do our best to enter:** Failure to respond to the Good News with active obedience to God’s voice ([4:1-2](Heb.4.1-Heb.4.2)) will have an outcome analogous to the outcome for the wilderness wanderers: **we will fall**.

**us . . . we . . . we:** Obedience is not simply a personal matter; God’s people have a communal responsibility for obedience and should support each other in that endeavor (cp. [3:13](Heb.3.13); [10:25](Heb.10.25); [12:15](Heb.12.15)).

Echoing the call to hear God’s voice ([3:7](Heb.3.7), [15](Heb.3.15); [4:7](Heb.4.7); quoted from [Ps 95:7](Ps.95.7)), the author gives a beautiful epigram on the power and penetration of God’s **word**.
**alive and powerful:** God’s word is an active, effective force. The word that created and governs the cosmos ([Heb 1:2-3](Heb.1.2-Heb.1.3)) can deal powerfully with people.

**the sharpest two-edged sword:** God’s word is able to penetrate the darkest recesses of people’s lives, exposing their **innermost thoughts and desires** (cp. [Eph 6:17](Eph.6.17); [Rev 1:16](Rev.1.16); [2:12](Rev.2.12), [16](Rev.2.16); [19:15](Rev.19.15)).
To be **naked and exposed** speaks figuratively of being vulnerable, helpless, or unprotected. The guilty are not able to hide from God’s penetrating word of judgment (cp. [Rev 3:17](Rev.3.17)).
These key verses conclude the exhortation begun at [3:1](Heb.3.1) and introduce the lengthy treatment of Jesus’ role as High Priest ([4:14–10:25](Heb.4.14-Heb.10.25)).
This verse effectively summarizes the whole message and challenge of Hebrews; the high priesthood of **Jesus the Son of God** is the basis for endurance in the Christian faith.

**a great High Priest:** Israel’s high priest was the main leader in the worship of God and the primary mediator between God and the people (see [Exod 31:10](Exod.31.10); [Lev 4:3](Lev.4.3); [2 Kgs 12:10](2Kgs.12.10); [2 Chr 26:20](2Chr.26.20)).

**who has entered heaven:** The earthly high priests entered God’s presence in the Most Holy Place once a year on the Day of Atonement ([Lev 16:1-25](Lev.16.1-Lev.16.25)). By contrast, Jesus, our High Priest, has entered God’s presence in heaven, and there he remains ([Heb 7:26](Heb.7.26); [9:11-12](Heb.9.11-Heb.9.12), [23-26](Heb.9.23-Heb.9.26)).

**let us hold firmly:** An enduring commitment to active belief in and allegiance to Jesus (see also [Col 2:19](Col.2.19); [2 Thes 2:15](2Thess.2.15); [Rev 2:13](Rev.2.13), [25](Rev.2.25); [3:11](Rev.3.11)).

Our High Priest **understands our weaknesses***,* our human pull toward sin, because **he faced all of the same testings we do**. He was tempted with all the essential aspects of sin, such as lust, greed, unforgiveness, and dishonesty. This makes him compassionate as our High Priest ([5:2](Heb.5.2)).

**yet he did not sin:** Jesus is unlike the earthly high priests, who had to make offerings for their own sins before they could make offerings for the people ([5:3](Heb.5.3); [7:26-28](Heb.7.26-Heb.7.28); see also [1 Pet 2:22-23](1Pet.2.22-1Pet.2.23)).
The verb translated **let us come** could be translated to indicate ongoing action: *let us continually come.*

As our compassionate High Priest, Jesus has opened the way for people to enter God’s presence **boldly** (see [6:19-20](Heb.6.19-Heb.6.20); [10:19-23](Heb.10.19-Heb.10.23)), where we can obtain his **mercy** and **grace to help us when we need it most**.

This section addresses the appointment of the Son of God as a superior High Priest. The focal text is [Ps 110:4](Ps.110.4), which reveals God’s oath that the Son would be a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.
**Every high priest:** This phrase introduces requirements for high priests in general.
**a man:** The high priest was one of the people, so Jesus had to become human (see [2:17-18](Heb.2.17-Heb.2.18)).

A second requirement for high priests was that they would **represent other people** by offering **sacrifices** on their behalf ([7:25-28](Heb.7.25-Heb.7.28)). Only the high priest could offer the sacrifice on the Day of Atonement ([Exod 29](Exod.29.1-Exod.29.46); [Lev 16:1-25](Lev.16.1-Lev.16.25)).
A high priest was **able to deal gently** with those who sin because **he himself** was **subject to the same weaknesses***,* i.e., he was sinful ([5:3](Heb.5.3); cp. [4:15](Heb.4.15)).
On the Day of Atonement the high priest was required to **offer sacrifices** for himself and his household prior to offering sacrifices for the people ([Lev 16:11](Lev.16.11)).
The role of **high priest** is by God’s appointment rather than human enlistment (see [Exod 28:1](Exod.28.1); [Lev 8:1-12](Lev.8.1-Lev.8.12); [Num 16:1-26](Num.16.1-Num.16.26)).

The author brings [Pss 2:7](Ps.2.7) and [110:4](Ps.110.4) together based on shared language—both passages have **God** speaking to his **Son**. The exalted Son, who came to earth as a human ([Heb 1–2](Heb.1.1-Heb.2.18)), is the one God has appointed to a unique high priesthood.
Jesus’ suffering was a foundation for his superior priesthood. The Son’s humiliation and suffering preceded his exaltation ([2:9](Heb.2.9); [Phil 2:5-11](Phil.2.5-Phil.2.11)).

The phrase **with a loud cry and tears** is probably an allusion to Christ’s suffering in the Garden (see [Matt 26:36-46](Matt.26.36-Matt.26.46); [Mark 14:32-42](Mark.14.32-Mark.14.42); [Luke 22:40-46](Luke.22.40-Luke.22.46)). **God heard his prayers** in the sense of affirming his righteousness and suitability for his role as high priest. Jesus’ faithful devotion is being presented as an example for the readers (cp. [Heb 12:2-3](Heb.12.2-Heb.12.3)).

**he learned obedience from the things he suffered:** Jesus was not disobedient before his suffering, but he walked his path of human experience—all the way to his death on the cross—in complete submission to the Father’s will. We are expected to travel the same path ([12:1-11](Heb.12.1-Heb.12.11)).

**God qualified him as a perfect High Priest:** As used in Hebrews, *perfect* means “complete” or “mature” (see [2:10](Heb.2.10); [5:14](Heb.5.14); [7:11](Heb.7.11); [9:9-11](Heb.9.9-Heb.9.11)). Jesus, through his sufferings, was qualified to be **the source of eternal salvation for all those who obey him**.
*High Priest* is not in the Greek text, but it is implied.
As the Son obeyed the Father ([5:8](Heb.5.8)), submitting completely to the Father’s will, so those who come to him for *salvation* must *obey him.*
**a High Priest in the order of Melchizedek:** See [7:1-28](Heb.7.1-Heb.7.28).

After beginning to discuss Jesus’ appointment as High Priest ([5:1-10](Heb.5.1-Heb.5.10)), the author confronts his audience with a series of exhortations ([5:11–6:20](Heb.5.11-Heb.6.20)). Such a shift in a sermon or discourse was meant to focus the hearers’ attention.
This exhortation deals with the recipients’ spiritual lethargy.
**spiritually dull:** The Greek term means “sluggish, dimwitted, negligent, lazy.”

Their lack of spiritual vitality was especially shocking since they had been **believers so long:** They ought to have been spiritual leaders who were **teaching others** from their wealth of knowledge and Christian experience.
**the basic things:** The most rudimentary aspects of the Christian faith (see [6:1-3](Heb.6.1-Heb.6.3)).
The imagery of **milk** and **solid food** (or *meat*) was used to distinguish basic from advanced education, and immature from mature students.
Being able **to recognize the difference between right and wrong** is a defining characteristic of spiritual maturity.

In light of the hearers’ immaturity ([5:11-14](Heb.5.11-Heb.5.14)), the author urges them to move beyond **basic teachings**. The six basic teachings here were all foundational elements of Jewish instruction. The author might be challenging them to move beyond these basic teachings to **further understanding** about the person of Christ, which he elaborates in [7:1–10:25](Heb.7.1-Heb.10.25).
**Let us go on:** Or *Let us be carried on,* suggesting that God initiates growth to maturity ([Phil 2:12-13](Phil.2.12-Phil.2.13)) and that it is an ongoing process.
**Repenting** and **faith** are the basic commitments that initiate a person to the new covenant and constitute the basic posture of a Christian’s life (see [Acts 20:21](Acts.20.21)).

The term **baptisms** (or *washings*) is plural, so it must mean more than just Christian baptism. Instruction about various washings was prevalent in first-century Judaism (see [Matt 15:2](Matt.15.2); [Mark 7:3](Mark.7.3)). The author might also have in mind the cleansing rituals of the Old Testament (cp. [Heb 9:13](Heb.9.13); [10:22](Heb.10.22)).

The **laying on of hands** was associated with healing ([Mark 5:22-23](Mark.5.22-Mark.5.23); [Luke 13:13](Luke.13.13)), ritual blessing ([Matt 19:13](Matt.19.13), [15](Matt.19.15)), reception of the Holy Spirit ([Acts 8:17](Acts.8.17); [9:17](Acts.9.17); [19:6](Acts.19.6)), and acknowledgement of a person’s ministry ([Acts 6:6](Acts.6.6); [13:3](Acts.13.3)).
**resurrection of the dead:** See “The Resurrection of the Dead” Theme Note.
**eternal judgment:** See [Rev 20:11-15](Rev.20.11-Rev.20.15).

The author is implicitly exhorting his readers to maturity, not only in their **understanding** but in everything (cp. [4:11](Heb.4.11); [5:14](Heb.5.14); [10:23-39](Heb.10.23-Heb.10.39); [12:1-13](Heb.12.1-Heb.12.13)).

This passage, one of the most difficult in the New Testament, gives a harsh warning about those who have left the Christian faith. Those who have fallen away from Christ and the church are like those who fell in the wilderness ([3:15-19](Heb.3.15-Heb.3.19)): The lack of faith shown in such apostasy results in devastating judgment (cp. [10:26-31](Heb.10.26-Heb.10.31)).
In Greek, the word **impossible** begins the sentence for emphasis—it absolutely cannot happen (see also [6:18](Heb.6.18); [10:4](Heb.10.4); [11:6](Heb.11.6)).
They were **once enlightened** when they “first learned about Christ” (see [10:32](Heb.10.32) and corresponding study note).
The **good things of heaven** might allude to the manna given from heaven ([Exod 16:4](Exod.16.4), [15](Exod.16.15); [Ps 78:24](Ps.78.24)) as an image of spiritual blessings.
**tasted the goodness of the word of God:** These people had heard the word of God preached ([2:3-4](Heb.2.3-Heb.2.4); [4:1-2](Heb.4.1-Heb.4.2)) and had seen its effects.

**the power of the age to come:** They had witnessed signs and wonders when they heard the Good News ([2:4](Heb.2.4); cp. [Exod 7:3-4](Exod.7.3-Exod.7.4); [Deut 7:19](Deut.7.19); [Pss 66:3](Ps.66.3); [77:15-20](Ps.77.15-Ps.77.20); [78:9-16](Ps.78.9-Ps.78.16); [1 Cor 10:1-13](1Cor.10.1-1Cor.10.13)).

**then turn** (or *fall*) **away:** The image is reminiscent of the wilderness wanderers who turned away from obeying God and fell in the desert ([3:17](Heb.3.17); [4:11](Heb.4.11); [Num 14:1-4](Num.14.1-Num.14.4), [29-30](Num.14.29-Num.14.30)).

**to bring such people back to repentance:** They had repented before, but had no fruit from their repentance ([Heb 6:7-8](Heb.6.7-Heb.6.8)). When people turn their back on Christ and his superior sacrifice, **it is impossible** for them to find any other means of repentance.

**Rejecting the Son of God** constitutes **nailing him to the cross once again**. Crucifixion was the ultimate instrument of rejection and humiliation in the Greco-Roman world and brought **public shame**. Those who turned away from Christ had in effect joined those who stood before the cross shouting insults, insisting that Jesus was not really the Messiah and Son of God but was instead worthy of shame (see [Matt 27:39-44](Matt.27.39-Matt.27.44)).

**ground:** Good, productive land is an image of blessing, contrasted with the curse of unproductive land that **bears thorns and thistles**. To **burn** such a field is an image of judgment ([2 Sam 23:4-7](2Sam.23.4-2Sam.23.7); [Isa 10:17](Isa.10.17); [33:12](Isa.33.12); [Ezek 19:12-13](Ezek.19.12-Ezek.19.13); [Matt 3:10](Matt.3.10)).

Having confronted his readers with a stern warning ([6:4-8](Heb.6.4-Heb.6.8)), the author now softens that warning by greeting them as **dear friends***,* expressing confidence in them, and giving them further encouragement.
**We are confident:** Skilled speakers and writers express confidence in those they address to motivate them (cp. [Rom 15:14](Rom.15.14)).

The author is confident that his hearers’ lives give evidence of a true relationship with God, including **salvation**. In the New Testament, salvation primarily refers to Christ’s work on the cross ([Heb 5:9-10](Heb.5.9-Heb.5.10); see also study note on 2:3); Hebrews places emphasis on the consummation of salvation at the end of the age ([9:28](Heb.9.28)).

**He will not forget how hard you have worked:** In showing that they love God and his people, their works bear witness to their true relationship with God ([Rom 2:6-7](Rom.2.6-Rom.2.7); [1 Cor 3:13-15](1Cor.3.13-1Cor.3.15); [Jas 2:14-20](Jas.2.14-Jas.2.20)). God remembers ([Exod 2:24](Exod.2.24); [1 Chr 16:15](1Chr.16.15); [Ps 106:45](Ps.106.45)) and acknowledges those who are truly his.

**keep on loving others** (literally *show the same eager commitment*): Love of other believers is a hallmark of genuine Christian faith ([Jas 2:15-16](Jas.2.15-Jas.2.16); [1 Jn 3:16-20](1John.3.16-1John.3.20)). Through diligence and focused commitment, they can **make** their **hope** in Christ absolutely **certain**. Assurance of salvation comes through perseverance.

A focused commitment ([6:10-11](Heb.6.10-Heb.6.11)) is the antidote to being **spiritually dull** ([5:11-12](Heb.5.11-Heb.5.12)). By loving God and others, we **follow the example** of great people of the faith. The author puts a great deal of emphasis on both **faith and endurance** as normal requirements for God’s people (see [11:4-38](Heb.11.4-Heb.11.38)).

This passage focuses on the reliability of God’s faithfulness to his promises. The theme of God’s oath is developed with an illustration ([6:13-15](Heb.6.13-Heb.6.15)), followed by a general principle ([6:16](Heb.6.16)), followed by the main point: God has sworn a significant oath ([6:17-18](Heb.6.17-Heb.6.18)), which gives us hope because it shows that Jesus is our permanent High Priest ([6:19-20](Heb.6.19-Heb.6.20)).

**Abraham** was the premier exemplar of faith: He continued to believe that God would give him a son, then was willing to sacrifice that son in obedience to God ([11:17-19](Heb.11.17-Heb.11.19); [Gen 15:1-5](Gen.15.1-Gen.15.5); [22:1-14](Gen.22.1-Gen.22.14)). In response to Abraham’s faith, **God took an oath,** assuring Abraham that he would **bless** him and **multiply** his **descendants**.
**what God had promised:** Through Isaac, God made Abraham into a great nation ([Exod 1:7](Exod.1.7)).

It is a general principle in human relationships that when **people take an oath***,* the **oath is binding**. If in human contexts oaths give assurance that something is true, an oath from God ought to inspire much greater confidence ([6:17-19](Heb.6.17-Heb.6.19)).
**someone greater than themselves:** Cp. [6:13](Heb.6.13).

**God also bound himself with an oath:** See [7:20-22](Heb.7.20-Heb.7.22). God’s oath makes it clear that **he would never change his mind** . . . **because it is impossible for God to lie** (see [Ps 110:4](Ps.110.4)).

We have **fled to him for refuge***,* like those in the Old Testament era who killed someone accidentally ([Num 35:9-34](Num.35.9-Num.35.34); [Deut 4:41-43](Deut.4.41-Deut.4.43)); Christ is like a city of refuge, where believers escape God’s wrath. Christ’s followers, therefore, have **great confidence**.
Christian **hope is a strong and trustworthy anchor for our souls**. In the first century, an anchor was an image of stability and safety.

**through the curtain:** A curtain separated the outer room of the sanctuary, into which only priests could go, from the inner room, the Most Holy Place ([Exod 25:10-40](Exod.25.10-Exod.25.40)). Only the high priest could go into the Most Holy Place, and only once per year on the Day of Atonement ([Exod 29](Exod.29.1-Exod.29.46); [Lev 16:1-25](Lev.16.1-Lev.16.25)). Because of Jesus’ extraordinary high priesthood, he **has already gone in there for us** into the presence of God as **our eternal High Priest***,* and he leads us in with him ([Heb 10:19-23](Heb.10.19-Heb.10.23)).
**the order of Melchizedek:** This phrase introduces the discussion in [7:1-28](Heb.7.1-Heb.7.28).
[Hebrews 7](Heb.7.1-Heb.7.28) develops the main topic introduced in [5:1-10](Heb.5.1-Heb.5.10): Jesus’ appointment as a high priest in the order of Melchizedek.
This section proclaims the superiority of Melchizedek’s priesthood over that of the Levites, based primarily on [Gen 14:17-20](Gen.14.17-Gen.14.20).
**king of . . . Salem:** See [Gen 14:18](Gen.14.18) and corresponding study note.
**also a priest of God Most High:** Unlike the Hebrew kings, Melchizedek combined the offices of king and priest, thus foreshadowing the Messiah.
**winning a great battle against the kings:** See [Gen 14:1-17](Gen.14.1-Gen.14.17).

Abraham was giving **a tenth** to the Lord by giving it to **Melchizedek***,* his priest. This act anticipates the giving of tithes under the law ([Lev 27:30](Lev.27.30), [32](Lev.27.32)) and becomes a key point in the author’s argument ([Heb 7:4](Heb.7.4)).
**Melchi-** (Hebrew *melek*) means **king**.
**-zedek** (Hebrew *tsedeq*) means **justice** or *righteousness*.

**Salem** (Hebrew *shalom*) means **peace**. It was common for rabbis to bring out the theological significance of a biblical figure’s name by making associations between the name and other Hebrew terms.

That we have **no record** of Melchizedek’s **father or mother or any of his ancestors** is significant in light of the ancestral requirement upon which the Levitical priesthood was based. He appears from nowhere—it is as though there is **no beginning or end to his life**. The author is interpreting [Gen 14:17-20](Gen.14.17-Gen.14.20) in light of [Ps 110:4](Ps.110.4), which also understands Melchizedek as representing an eternal priesthood.
**He remains a priest forever:** This contrasts with a Levite, whose priesthood ended when he died ([Heb 7:8](Heb.7.8), [23](Heb.7.23)).
**resembling the Son of God:** Melchizedek was not an Old Testament appearance of Jesus. Rather, his priesthood and that of Jesus had characteristics in common, in light of [Ps 110:4](Ps.110.4).

The point of this section ([7:1-10](Heb.7.1-Heb.7.10)) is to have the readers **consider** . . . **how great this Melchizedek was** by comparing him to the descendants of Levi. Melchizedek was so great that **Abraham** gave him **a tenth** of the spoils of **battle** ([Gen 14:20](Gen.14.20)).
Collecting the **tithe** was a requirement and an honor for the **priests** under **the law of Moses** ([Num 18:21-32](Num.18.21-Num.18.32)).
**from the rest of the people of Israel:** The reference is to the people of Israel as a whole.

Although **Melchizedek** was **not a descendant of Levi***,* he **collected a tenth from Abraham***,* the ancestor of the Levites. This demonstrates Melchizedek’s eminence over both Abraham and his descendants, including the priests ([Heb 7:8-10](Heb.7.8-Heb.7.10)).

**Melchizedek placed a blessing upon Abraham:** [Gen 14:19-20](Gen.14.19-Gen.14.20); this is an example of the kind of blessing that a superior would give a subordinate—e.g., a father would bless his son, and a priest would bless his people ([Gen 49:1-28](Gen.49.1-Gen.49.28); [Num 6:22-27](Num.6.22-Num.6.27)). The power to give a blessing demonstrates that Melchizedek **is greater than** Abraham.
Melchizedek’s “immortality” ([7:3](Heb.7.3)) is one aspect of his superiority to the Levites: The Levites **are men who die***,* but Melchizedek **lives on**.

**we might even say:** The author recognizes that what he is about to say, that the **Levites** . . . **paid a tithe to Melchizedek***,* is not literally true, since **Levi wasn’t born yet**. Abraham represented all his descendants in paying his tithe to Melchizedek. Levi was united with Abraham because **the seed from which he came was in Abraham’s body**. All the people issuing from Abraham were one with him. Thus, his act could be considered their act.

Having argued for Melchizedek’s superiority to the Levites ([7:1-10](Heb.7.1-Heb.7.10)), the author now argues that Jesus, our high priest like Melchizedek, is also superior to the Levitical priests of the old covenant.

**Perfection** in Hebrews does not mean *flawless,* but *reaching a desired goal* (see study note on 5:9). The priesthood under the old covenant could not achieve all that **God intended** for a covenant relationship with his people. That is why God needed **to establish a different priesthood**.

According to the law given to Moses, the appointed priests were descendants of Aaron ([Exod 28:41-43](Exod.28.41-Exod.28.43); [29:9](Exod.29.9)). The **priesthood is changed** because Jesus is now the High Priest. Thus, God himself had **changed** the **law** concerning priests.
Jesus **belongs to a different tribe:** Under the old covenant, priests came from the tribe of Levi, whereas Jesus was from **the tribe of Judah**.

**This change** of how God appoints priests ([7:11-14](Heb.7.11-Heb.7.14)) has been made **very clear** by the appointment of Jesus as a **different priest**. He, **like Melchizedek***,* is **a priest forever:** Jesus’ resurrection from the dead shows that he has **the power of a life that cannot be destroyed**. Because his priesthood **in the order of Melchizedek** is superior to that of the Levites ([7:1-10](Heb.7.1-Heb.7.10)), he supersedes them as priest.
**The old requirement about the priesthood** was membership in the family of Aaron (see [Exod 28:41-43](Exod.28.41-Exod.28.43)).
**set aside:** See [Heb 7:15-17](Heb.7.15-Heb.7.17).
**because it was weak and useless:** As explained in the verses that follow ([7:19-28](Heb.7.19-Heb.7.28)).

The weakness of the priesthood under the old covenant is highlighted in that those priests died (thus discontinuing their office) and were themselves sinful. In contrast, Jesus, the new High Priest, never sinned and conquered death, making him a more effective and permanent High Priest.

**the law never made anything perfect:** The law never accomplished what God planned to accomplish through the superior high priesthood of Jesus—namely, completely removing sin and guaranteeing eternal salvation. This gives believers **confidence in a better hope** in relationship with God. We can **draw near to God** without fearing condemnation.
**This new system** refers to God’s way of appointing a priest.
God’s **solemn oath** is expressed in the quote from [Ps 110:4](Ps.110.4).

Legally, **the one who guarantees** (literally *the guarantee* or *the guarantor*) refers to the person who bears the risk of another person’s investment or debt. Because of God’s **oath***,* Jesus’ priesthood is unassailable, so our **covenant** relationship **with God** is secure. Having Jesus as the guarantor makes the new covenant **better**.

Of necessity, the old covenant had a succession of **many priests** because each of them died. In contrast, Jesus’ **priesthood lasts forever** (literally *is permanent*): This term refers to something that cannot be changed, such as the sun’s daily trek through the sky or the constant turning of the seasons.
**able, once and forever, to save:** Since Jesus **lives forever***,* the salvation he brings also lasts forever. To draw near to an eternal God, we need an eternal priest.

Jesus will **intercede** or *appeal* to God for us as our High Priest of the new covenant, and his intercession is never-ending (see [9:11-28](Heb.9.11-Heb.9.28); [10:21-22](Heb.10.21-Heb.10.22); [Rom 8:31-34](Rom.8.31-Rom.8.34)).

Jesus is **unstained by sin** and **set apart from sinners** (cp. [4:15](Heb.4.15)), which makes him superior to the priests of the old covenant, who had to deal with **their own sins** as well as those **of the people** (see also [5:1-3](Heb.5.1-Heb.5.3)).
**has been given the highest place of honor in heaven:** This is an affirmation of his uniqueness as High Priest (cp. [2:9](Heb.2.9); [5:9](Heb.5.9); [Phil 2:5-11](Phil.2.5-Phil.2.11)).
**once for all:** This does not mean *once for all people* but rather *once, never to be repeated.*
This verse echoes [5:1-3](Heb.5.1-Heb.5.3) and sums up the entire discussion of Christ’s appointment as High Priest ([5:1-10](Heb.5.1-Heb.5.10); [7:1-28](Heb.7.1-Heb.7.28)).
**Limited by human weakness** refers primarily to human sinfulness and mortality ([5:2-3](Heb.5.2-Heb.5.3); [7:18](Heb.7.18), [23-27](Heb.7.23-Heb.7.27)).
**God appointed his Son with an oath:** See [Ps 110:4](Ps.110.4), the key Old Testament passage behind [Heb 7:11-28](Heb.7.11-Heb.7.28).
**perfect . . . forever:** The words **High Priest** are not in the Greek text but are implied in the context.

In Hebrews, the term **perfect** means *complete* or *mature* (see [2:10](Heb.2.10); [5:9](Heb.5.9); [7:11](Heb.7.11); [9:9-11](Heb.9.9-Heb.9.11)); the Son, through his sacrificial death and resurrection, has become completely qualified to serve as our eternal High Priest, and his priesthood lasts **forever**.
This passage on Jesus’ superior offering argues that his ministry as the heavenly High Priest is superior to that of earthly priests.
The first two verses of ch [8](Heb.8.1-Heb.8.13) transition from the discussion just completed and anticipate the discussion to come.
**Here is the main point:** The author is referring back to the appointment of Jesus as a superior High Priest ([5:1-10](Heb.5.1-Heb.5.10); [7:1-28](Heb.7.1-Heb.7.28)).

**he ministers in the heavenly Tabernacle** (or *tent;* also in [8:5](Heb.8.5)): This anticipates the theme of Jesus’ superior offering that is covered in the rest of this section ([8:3–10:18](Heb.8.3-Heb.10.18)). Unlike the Levitical priests who served in an earthly tent or building, Jesus’ sacrifice is superior because he serves in **the true place of worship***,* the very presence of God in heaven ([8:5](Heb.8.5); [9:11](Heb.9.11), [24](Heb.9.24); [10:12](Heb.10.12)).
**every high priest is required to offer gifts and sacrifices:** Making offerings is a general requirement of priests, so Jesus also had to offer a sacrifice.
This verse reiterates what is stated in the first verse of the previous discussion ([5:1](Heb.5.1)), indicating another major movement in the book.

**If he were here on earth:** Under the old order Jesus **would not even be a priest***,* as previously discussed (see [7:13-14](Heb.7.13-Heb.7.14)). But Jesus is in heaven, which makes his priestly service distinct from and superior to that of the priests of the old covenant ([8:5](Heb.8.5); [9:11](Heb.9.11), [24](Heb.9.24); [10:12](Heb.10.12)).

**a copy, a shadow:** The earthly place of worship was an imitation that pointed to **the real one in heaven**. That is why **God** warned **Moses** to make it **according to the pattern** (see [Exod 25:40](Exod.25.40); [26:30](Exod.26.30); cp. [Acts 7:44](Acts.7.44)). Judaism and early Christianity both spoke of a heavenly Temple within a heavenly Jerusalem, which would come down to earth at the end of the age (see [Rev 21:2](Rev.21.2)). Hebrews suggests that this heavenly place of worship was shown to Moses so he would know how to build the earthly Tabernacle. It is the heavenly Temple, however, in which Jesus ministers as High Priest.
**the one who mediates:** A mediator works with two parties to bring them to agreement. Christ’s work of sacrifice established the **covenant** relationship between people and God.
**a far better covenant with God:** See “The New Covenant” Theme Note. This covenant is better because it is **based on better promises** (see [8:7-13](Heb.8.7-Heb.8.13)).

The author quotes [Jer 31:31-34](Jer.31.31-Jer.31.34), an Old Testament prophecy concerning the new covenant that includes a number of striking promises. Establishing the superiority of the new covenant lays a foundation for the argument in [Heb 9:1–10:18](Heb.9.1-Heb.10.18) that the Son’s offering under the new covenant was superior to the offerings of the old covenant.
The **first covenant***,* made at Sinai, was not **faultless**. It was not the end of God’s plan, because it didn’t solve human weaknesses (see [7:11-28](Heb.7.11-Heb.7.28); [8:9](Heb.8.9)).
**found fault with the people:** Because the people were unable to keep the terms of the old covenant (see study note on 8:7), God made a **new covenant**.
God **made** a covenant **with their ancestors** at Sinai ([Exod 19:1-8](Exod.19.1-Exod.19.8); [24:7-8](Exod.24.7-Exod.24.8); [34:27-28](Exod.34.27-Exod.34.28); [Deut 4:13](Deut.4.13)).

**I took them by the hand:** In rescuing his people from **the land of Egypt***,* God **led them** as a parent might lead a child that could not fend for itself (see [Exod 12–14](Exod.12.1-Exod.14.31)).
**They did not remain faithful:** See [Heb 3:7-19](Heb.3.7-Heb.3.19); [Num 14:1-38](Num.14.1-Num.14.38); [Deut 9](Deut.9.1-Deut.9.29); [Ps 106](Ps.106.1-Ps.106.48).

**so I turned my back on them:** The covenant warned that if the people turned away, God would turn away from them (see [Deut 28:15-68](Deut.28.15-Deut.28.68); [30:11-20](Deut.30.11-Deut.30.20); [1 Kgs 8:22-53](1Kgs.8.22-1Kgs.8.53); [2 Chr 6:12-42](2Chr.6.12-2Chr.6.42)).

Under the old covenant, the people were commanded to take the words of the law to heart ([Deut 32:46](Deut.32.46)), and the kings of Israel and Judah were judged on whether or not they followed the law of God wholeheartedly ([2 Kgs 10:31](2Kgs.10.31); [2 Chr 31:21](2Chr.31.21)). A difference in the **new covenant** is that God’s **laws** would be in people’s **minds** and **on their hearts**. People would have renewed hearts and minds, with God’s law as an intrinsic, internal motivation.
All those in the new covenant **know the** **LORD***;* intimate personal relationship with the Lord is in the very nature of the new covenant.

A final characteristic of the new covenant is that God would **forgive their wickedness** and **never again remember their sins**. The blood of Jesus cleanses his people completely from sin ([9:13-15](Heb.9.13-Heb.9.15); [10:14-18](Heb.10.14-Heb.10.18), [22](Heb.10.22); [1 Jn 1:7](1John.1.7)).

The word *new* in **“new” covenant** emphasizes that, once God had enacted this covenant, the Sinai covenant was considered *old* or **obsolete** and was thus **out of date**. Its time of usefulness was over and its termination was imminent.

This section argues that Christ’s death, the sacrifice in the new covenant, is superior to the sacrifices in the old covenant. In [9:1-10](Heb.9.1-Heb.9.10), the author describes aspects of worship under the **regulations** of the old covenant (see [Exod 28–29](Exod.28.1-Exod.29.46); [Lev 1–10](Lev.1.1-Lev.10.20); [16:1–17:16](Lev.16.1-Lev.17.16)). In [Heb 9:11–10:18](Heb.9.11-Heb.10.18), these regulations are contrasted with Christ’s superior offering.
These verses describe the **Tabernacle**, Israel’s **place of worship** before the Temple was constructed.
Israel’s **Tabernacle** was a tent with **two rooms** (see [Exod 25–31](Exod.25.1-Exod.31.18); [35:1–40:38](Exod.35.1-Exod.40.38)).
The priests went into the **Holy Place** daily in their ritual duties ([Heb 9:6](Heb.9.6); see [Exod 28:43](Exod.28.43); [Num 28:3-8](Num.28.3-Num.28.8)).

At the back of the first room of the Tabernacle was a **curtain** that separated the first room from the **second room called the Most Holy Place** ([Exod 26:31-33](Exod.26.31-Exod.26.33)). This curtain was a sacred barrier: Only the high priest could go behind it into the Most Holy Place, and only once a year on the Day of Atonement ([Heb 9:7](Heb.9.7); see [Exod 30:6](Exod.30.6), [10](Exod.30.10); [Lev 16:2-34](Lev.16.2-Lev.16.34); [23:27-32](Lev.23.27-Lev.23.32)).

The **gold incense altar** probably stood just outside the inner curtain ([Exod 30:1-10](Exod.30.1-Exod.30.10)); its location is ambiguous at points in the Old Testament, but it was closely associated with the Most Holy Place ([Exod 30:6](Exod.30.6); [Lev 16:13](Lev.16.13); [1 Kgs 6:22](1Kgs.6.22)).
Since it represented the presence of God, the **Ark of the Covenant** was the most important item in the Tabernacle (see [Exod 25:10-22](Exod.25.10-Exod.25.22)).
The **gold jar containing manna** was a reminder of God’s provision in the wilderness ([Exod 16:32-34](Exod.16.32-Exod.16.34)).
**Aaron’s staff that sprouted leaves** (see [Num 17:1-11](Num.17.1-Num.17.11)) was a reminder not to rebel against God’s chosen leaders ([Num 17:10](Num.17.10); cp. [Heb 13:17](Heb.13.17)).

The **stone tablets of the covenant** held the Ten Commandments and were to remind the people of the terms by which they were to live out the covenant ([Exod 25:16](Exod.25.16); [31:18](Exod.31.18); [Deut 9:9–10:5](Deut.9.9-Deut.10.5)).

**The cherubim of divine glory** were statues of angels formed into the Ark’s cover. This category of angels is especially associated with God’s glorious presence ([Gen 3:24](Gen.3.24); [Pss 80:1](Ps.80.1); [99:1](Ps.99.1); [Isa 37:16](Isa.37.16)). The **Ark’s cover** itself was **the place of atonement***,* on which the blood from the Day of Atonement sacrifice was to be sprinkled ([Lev 16:14-16](Lev.16.14-Lev.16.16)).
**But we cannot explain these things in detail now:** The main focus of the discussion is the offering of sacrifices under the old covenant ([Heb 9:6-10](Heb.9.6-Heb.9.10)).

The worship practices in the Holy Place, the **first room** of the Tabernacle ([9:2](Heb.9.2)), were the duty of the priests, who kept the lamps lit and the sacred loaves of bread replenished ([Exod 27:20-21](Exod.27.20-Exod.27.21); [Lev 24:8](Lev.24.8)).

The yearly duty was carried out on the Day of Atonement, when **the high priest** offered sacrifices for **the sins** not covered by other sacrifices during the previous year ([Lev 16:1-25](Lev.16.1-Lev.16.25)).
**was not freely open:** Free entrance into the presence of God was not available to all of the people under the old covenant system.

The outer room of **the Tabernacle***,* which served as a sacred barrier keeping the people from the presence of God in **the Most Holy Place***,* was symbolic of the whole system. Under that system, people were kept out of God’s presence rather than led into it.

**This is an illustration:** The problem with **the gifts and sacrifices** of the old covenant is that they were **not able to cleanse the consciences of the people**—they could not remove people’s guilt before a holy God (cp. [9:14](Heb.9.14); [10:2](Heb.10.2), [22](Heb.10.22); [13:18](Heb.13.18)).

The **old system** dealt only with **physical regulations***,* and it could not deal with the condition of the heart ([8:10](Heb.8.10); [10:21-24](Heb.10.21-Heb.10.24)). Consequently, it was provisional, only intended to last until Christ could come and establish a **better system** ([9:11–10:18](Heb.9.11-Heb.10.18)).

The author now contrasts the old system ([9:1-10](Heb.9.1-Heb.9.10)) with the superior sacrifice made by Christ as High Priest: The blood of Christ’s offering was his own blood, not the blood of animals ([9:13-22](Heb.9.13-Heb.9.22); cp. [9:7](Heb.9.7)); Christ’s offering was made in the heavenly Tabernacle, not the earthly one ([9:23-24](Heb.9.23-Heb.9.24); cp. [9:1-5](Heb.9.1-Heb.9.5)); and Christ’s offering, rather than being made continually, was made just one time ([9:25–10:18](Heb.9.25-Heb.10.18); cp. [7:27](Heb.7.27); [9:6-7](Heb.9.6-Heb.9.7)).

**Christ has now become the High Priest over all the good things** of the new covenant. He was appointed by God in accord with [Ps 110:4](Ps.110.4) ([Heb 5:1-10](Heb.5.1-Heb.5.10); [7:1-28](Heb.7.1-Heb.7.28)) and offered a superior offering.
**that have come:** Some manuscripts read *that are about to come,* either from the perspective of the old covenant era or looking forward to the culmination of God’s plan in the future.

Christ’s sacrifice is superior because of where it was made: in **that greater, more perfect Tabernacle in heaven** rather than the earthly Tabernacle (see [8:5](Heb.8.5) and corresponding study note).
Christ’s offering is superior because it was made **with his own blood** rather than **the blood of goats and calves** (e.g., cp. [Lev 16:3-5](Lev.16.3-Lev.16.5)).

Christ’s offering is superior because **he entered the Most Holy Place once for all time**. Unlike the sacrifices in the old covenant, which had to be made year after year ([Heb 10:1](Heb.10.1)), Jesus’ sacrificial death only had to be made once and was decisive in securing **our redemption forever**.
The **ashes of a heifer** were used with water to **cleanse people’s bodies from ceremonial impurity** (see [Num 19](Num.19.1-Num.19.22)).

**how much more:** This is an argument from lesser to greater, a traditional Jewish rhetorical strategy; the logic is that if something is true in a lesser situation, it will be even more true in a greater situation (see also [2:1-4](Heb.2.1-Heb.2.4); [12:25-29](Heb.12.25-Heb.12.29)). If the blood of animals had some effect in cleansing, the blood of Christ will be much more effective.
**will purify our consciences:** Christ’s sacrifice, unlike the sacrifices of the old covenant, removes the paralyzing guilt that keeps us from God by decisively cleansing us **from sinful deeds**.

**the one who mediates:** This term refers to an arbiter in a difficult legal dispute or political disagreement. In the old covenant, Moses and the angels were understood as mediators between God and the people ([Gal 3:19-20](Gal.3.19-Gal.3.20)). In the **new covenant***,* Christ **mediates** the relationship between **God and people** by his sacrificial death ([Heb 8:6](Heb.8.6); [12:24](Heb.12.24); [Rom 6:23](Rom.6.23); [1 Tim 2:5](1Tim.2.5); [1 Pet 3:18](1Pet.3.18)) and ongoing intercession ([Heb 7:25](Heb.7.25)).

The author gives a general principle about the nature of wills or covenants ([9:16-17](Heb.9.16-Heb.9.17)), which he then expounds in light of the inauguration of the first covenant ([9:18-22](Heb.9.18-Heb.9.22)).
**was put into effect:** [Exod 24:3-8](Exod.24.3-Exod.24.8) records Moses’ inauguration of the old covenant with the blood of the sacrifice.
Hebrews alone among ancient sources states that Moses sprinkled **the book of God’s law** (cp. [Exod 24:6-8](Exod.24.6-Exod.24.8)).

**Hyssop branches** have blue flowers and strongly aromatic leaves; they were used with sacrifices for cleansing ([Exod 12:22](Exod.12.22); [Lev 14:4](Lev.14.4); [Num 19:6](Num.19.6), [18](Num.19.18)).

**“This blood confirms the covenant God has made with you”** ([Exod 24:8](Exod.24.8)): Jesus used similar language at the Lord’s Supper, referring to his own death ([Matt 26:28](Matt.26.28); [Mark 14:24](Mark.14.24); [1 Cor 11:25](1Cor.11.25)).
**he sprinkled blood:** See [Exod 24:3-8](Exod.24.3-Exod.24.8); [Lev 16:14-19](Lev.16.14-Lev.16.19).

Many of the rituals of cleansing in **the law of Moses** involved the death of a sacrificial animal; **blood** was involved both in the rites of cleansing (see [Exod 29:12](Exod.29.12); [30:10](Exod.30.10); [Lev 4:6](Lev.4.6), [17](Lev.4.17); [16:14-19](Lev.16.14-Lev.16.19); [Num 19:4](Num.19.4)) and in making atonement (see [Lev 16](Lev.16.1-Lev.16.34)). The **shedding** of Christ’s blood established the new covenant, providing permanent purification and complete **forgiveness** of sins ([Heb 8:12](Heb.8.12); [10:15-18](Heb.10.15-Heb.10.18); [Matt 26:28](Matt.26.28); [Eph 1:7](Eph.1.7)).

This verse argues from lesser to greater (see study note on 9:14). Just as **heaven** is greater than the earthly **Tabernacle***,* so Christ’s sacrifice **had to be** . . . **far better** than the earthly sacrifices.
**copies of things in heaven:** See study note on Heb 8:5.

**in heaven, had to be purified:** Just as the Tabernacle had to be cleansed because of the sin of the Israelites ([Lev 16:16-19](Lev.16.16-Lev.16.19)), the heavenly Tabernacle required that the uncleanness be removed from those who would enter heaven under the new covenant.

Under the new covenant, **Christ** did not offer his sacrifice in the earthly Tabernacle. Rather, he **entered into** the very presence of God in **heaven** to act **on our behalf**. His sacrifice makes him a much better mediator to bring us into a right relationship with God ([2 Cor 5:19-21](2Cor.5.19-2Cor.5.21)).
Under the old covenant, the sacrifice on the Day of Atonement had to be made **again and again** ([Lev 16:29-34](Lev.16.29-Lev.16.34)). Christ’s superior sacrifice was made **once for all time**.

**If that had been necessary:** The author makes an argument using *reductio ad absurdum* (reduction to absurdity), logically showing that Christ’s one-time sacrifice must be permanently effective. Since Christ himself is the **sacrifice** as well as the high priest, if his offering were made every year as with the earthly high priests, he would have to **die again and again**. But of course this is absurd; so, clearly, Christ died **once for all time** . . . **to remove sin**.

Christ’s first coming was to **take away the sins of many people**. When **he will come again***,* it will not be to deal with sins, since that has already been accomplished. Instead, he will **bring salvation to all who are eagerly waiting for him** (see study note on Gal 5:5).

**The old system under the law of Moses** (literally *The law*), like the Tabernacle itself ([8:5](Heb.8.5)), **was only a shadow, a dim preview** of a greater reality—namely, **the good things** that Christ inaugurated in the new covenant. Under the old covenant, **sacrifices** had to be **repeated again and again** because they were not able to cleanse worshipers permanently or in such a way that they could come into the presence of God perpetually.
The perpetual nature of the sacrifices demonstrates their inadequacy. **If** the sacrifices of the old covenant had offered true, lasting purity, they **would have stopped**.
**their feelings of guilt would have disappeared:** Cp. [9:9](Heb.9.9), [14](Heb.9.14); [10:22](Heb.10.22); [13:18](Heb.13.18).
**Instead** of removing guilt, the ongoing sacrifices **actually reminded** those who wished to come near to God, **year after year***,* that they were guilty before God.

The **blood of bulls and goats** in the sacrifices of the old covenant offered a degree of cleansing ([9:13](Heb.9.13), [23](Heb.9.23)), but that cleansing was limited in that it could not **take away sins**. It could not eradicate sin in a way that would offer permanent cleansing and peace with God (see [Acts 10:36](Acts.10.36); [Rom 5:1](Rom.5.1); [11:26-27](Rom.11.26-Rom.11.27)).

These verses quote [Ps 40:6-8](Ps.40.6-Ps.40.8). [Psalm 40](Ps.40.1-Ps.40.17) is a hymn of praise to God in which the psalmist confesses his desire to do God’s will. The author of Hebrews understands **Christ** to be the speaker.

**But you have given me a body to offer:** God had prepared the psalmist to be obedient, ready to do God’s will; Hebrews now applies this idea to Christ. For Hebrews, the preparation of a human *body*, specifically Christ’s body, shows that God would use it as a superior sacrifice.
The author follows the flow of thought in the psalm with great precision.
**First, Christ said, “You did not want animal sacrifices . . .”:** The author of Hebrews understands this as God’s rejection of the old system of sacrifices.
**Then he said, “Look, I have come to do your will”:** The author of Hebrews takes this to be Christ’s willingness to be the supreme sacrifice for sins.

The author of Hebrews concludes that because of Christ’s sacrifice, God has canceled the first covenant—**God’s will***,* as shown by [Ps 40:6-8](Ps.40.6-Ps.40.8), was that Christ would die for sins as a **sacrifice***,* and this only had to be done **once for all time**.
Christ’s superior offering was decisive, in contrast with the sacrifices made by the priests of the old covenant.
**the priest stands:** See [Deut 18:5](Deut.18.5).
**day after day:** E.g., [2 Chr 13:11](2Chr.13.11).
Christ’s sacrifice contrasts with that of the earthly high priests in that he **offered himself to God as a** . . . **sacrifice***,* rather than offering animal sacrifices.

After the sacrifice was accomplished, **he sat down in the place of honor** (see [Ps 110:1](Ps.110.1)). Instead of standing daily like the priests of the old covenant ([Heb 10:11](Heb.10.11)), **he waits until his enemies are humbled and made a footstool under his feet** ([Ps 110:1](Ps.110.1)).
**made perfect:** See study notes on 7:11, 28.
**those who are being made holy:** What the author has in mind is complete purification from sins.
